text:
255. Doubt manifests itself through characteristic patterns of behavior, but these behaviors qualify as manifestations of doubt only when they occur in particular circumstances. If someone declared that he doubted the existence of his hands, and if he then proceeded to examine them repeatedly from various angles, attempting to verify that mirrors or other deceptive mechanisms were not generating the visual appearances, we would face uncertainty about whether to classify such behavior as genuine doubting. We might characterize his conduct as resembling doubt-behavior in certain respects, but the activity in which he was engaged would differ fundamentally from our own practice of doubting.

256. Language-games are not static; they undergo modification over time.

257. If someone informed me that he doubted whether he possessed a body, my inclination would be to regard him as cognitively impaired. Yet I would not know what procedure to follow in attempting to convince him that he did possess a body. Moreover, if I happened to say something that eliminated his doubt, I would remain ignorant of the mechanism by which this occurred and the explanation for its success.

258. The proper use of the sentence "I have a body" remains unclear to me. This uncertainty does not apply without qualification to the proposition that I have always existed on or near the earth's surface.

259. Someone who doubted whether the earth had existed for a hundred years might harbor either a scientific doubt or a philosophical one.

260. I prefer to reserve the expression "I know" for those cases where it functions within ordinary linguistic practice.

261. At present, I cannot formulate a reasonable doubt concerning the earth's existence during the past hundred years.

262. One can imagine a person raised under highly unusual circumstances who received instruction to the effect that the earth came into being fifty years ago, and who consequently believed this claim. We might attempt to instruct him by saying that the earth has existed for a much longer period. In doing so, we would be attempting to provide him with our picture of the world. This process would proceed through something resembling persuasion rather than demonstration.

263. The schoolchild believes what his teachers tell him and what appears in his textbooks.

264. One could imagine Moore captured by a tribe unfamiliar with modern civilization, with the tribe members expressing suspicion that he arrived from some location between the earth and the moon. Moore informs them that he knows he has never been to such a place, but he cannot supply them with grounds for his certainty, given that they possess fantastic ideas about human capacities for flight and lack any knowledge of physics. Such a situation would constitute an appropriate occasion for making that statement.

265. Yet what does such a statement communicate beyond the claim "I have never been to such and such a place, and I possess compelling grounds for believing this"?

266. One would still need to specify what qualifies as compelling grounds.

267. "I don't merely receive a visual impression of a tree: I know that it is a tree."

268. "I know that this is a hand."—And what constitutes a hand?—"Well, this, for instance."

269. Am I more certain that I have never been on the moon than that I have never been in Bulgaria? What accounts for this degree of sureness? I know that I have never traveled anywhere in that geographical region—for instance, I have never visited the Balkans.

270. "I possess compelling grounds for my certitude." Such grounds render the certitude objective rather than merely subjective.

271. What constitutes a telling ground for some proposition is not something I determine through decision.

272. To say "I know" is to say that I am familiar with something as a certainty.

273. But when does one properly say of something that it is certain? Disagreement can arise concerning whether something qualifies as certain; what I have in mind is the question of when something is objectively certain. Countless general empirical propositions count as certain for us.

274. One such proposition is that if someone's arm is severed, it will not regenerate. Another is that if someone's head is severed, he dies and will never return to life. Experience can be said to teach us these propositions. It does not, however, teach them to us in isolation. Rather, experience teaches us a host of interdependent propositions. Were they isolated from one another, I might doubt them, given that I would then lack experience bearing on them.

275. If experience constitutes the ground of our certainty, then the relevant experience is necessarily past experience. Moreover, the experience in question is not exclusively my own; I acquire knowledge from the experience of others as well.

One might respond that it is experience itself that leads us to grant credence to other persons. But what experience provides me with grounds for believing that anatomy and physiology texts do not contain falsehoods? It remains true, nevertheless, that this trust receives backing from my own experience.

276. We believe, so to speak, that a great edifice exists, and we then observe, at various times, one small corner of it or another.

277. "I can't help believing..."

278. "I am comfortable that matters stand thus."

279. It is entirely certain that automobiles do not grow from the earth. We have the conviction that if someone could believe the contrary, he could believe anything that we regard as false and could question everything that we hold to be sure. But how does this single belief connect with all the rest? We want to say that someone capable of believing such a thing does not accept our entire system of verification. A human being acquires this system through observation and instruction. I intentionally refrain from saying "learns."

280. After he has observed certain things and received certain instruction, he is no longer in a position to doubt whether such-and-such is the case.

281. I, L.W., believe—am certain—that my friend does not have sawdust in his body or in his head, despite possessing no direct sensory evidence to the contrary. I am sure by reason of what has been communicated to me, what I have read, and my own experience. To harbor doubts about this matter would strike me as madness. This conviction is, of course, also in agreement with what others believe, and I agree with them.

282. I cannot claim to possess good grounds for the opinion that cats do not grow on trees or that I had a father and a mother. If someone doubts such matters, how could this doubt have originated? Through his never having believed, from the outset, that he had parents? But is such a scenario conceivable unless he received explicit instruction to this effect?

283. Doubt requires a foundation just as belief does. Someone who doubted everything we consider certain would need to have learned this doubting somewhere. The doubt itself would have to have been acquired.

284. People have killed animals since the earliest times, employing their furs for clothing, their bones for tools. With complete confidence they have inferred from the animal's behavior that it suffered pain, that it was alive, that it was dead. These inferences form the foundation upon which more sophisticated judgments rest. No one ever instructed primitive humans that the animal was dead; they observed and drew conclusions. But is it correct to say they drew conclusions? Does a conclusion require formulation in language?

285. If someone searched for something in his room and found it in a drawer, that would not ordinarily constitute grounds for saying "I knew it was in the drawer." Yet he might say "I thought it might be there." Must one think before one can know?

286. What we call "knowing" stands in various relationships to what we call "being certain," "believing," "trusting."

287. "I can't be making a mistake about it"—that is an important language-game. But does it follow that one is infallible about such matters?

288. I am certain of it does not mean that I am infallible about it. The proposition admits of being used differently in different language-games.

289. "I know that I am a human being." In order to see how unclear the sense of this proposition is, consider its negation. One might say "I know that I am not a machine," but this functions differently.

290. I know where I have spent the past hour. I acquired this knowledge not through instruction but through immediate experience. But can I say I know it with the same certainty that two and two make four?
